subject: ela
description: Students plan and evaluate spoken presentations that report claims and findings. They sequence ideas in a logical order, support a claim with pertinent descriptions, facts, and details, and recognize when supporting evidence is relevant or off topic. They also identify and judge effective delivery: appropriate eye contact, adequate volume, and clear pronunciation. Because this is a speaking and listening standard, items are built around scenarios the student needs nothing external to understand. Each item embeds the full stimulus it depends on, such as a presentation outline, a transcript of what a speaker said, a set of note cards, or a short description of a speaker's delivery. Difficulty scales by the length and complexity of that stimulus, by whether the task asks the student to identify, analyze, or evaluate, and by how much inference is required to judge logical sequence, relevance of evidence, or quality of delivery.
subSkills: Sequence ideas in a logical order so a presentation has a clear beginning, middle, and end and each point builds on the last
State a clear claim and distinguish it from the facts and details that support it
Select descriptions, facts, and details that are pertinent to the claim and remove evidence that is off topic or irrelevant
Recognize when a supporting detail is relevant, accurate, and specific versus vague, unrelated, or merely an opinion
Identify and evaluate effective delivery features: appropriate eye contact, adequate volume, and clear pronunciation
Judge whether a speaker's delivery and organization help the audience follow and believe the findings, and suggest a specific improvement

problemArchetypes.name: Order the presentation logically
problemArchetypes.example: Read these four points a student wants to make in a presentation about recycling at school: (1) 'Other schools that started programs cut their trash in half.' (2) 'Our school should start a recycling program.' (3) 'Right now we throw away hundreds of bottles every week.' (4) 'Here is how we could set up bins in each hallway.' Which order presents the claim and findings most logically? Answer: 2, 3, 1, 4, because the speaker states the claim, shows the problem, gives evidence it works, then proposes the plan.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the claim versus the supporting detail
problemArchetypes.example: Read this part of a presentation: 'School should start an hour later. Studies of middle schools found that students who started at 8:30 scored higher on tests and missed fewer days.' Which sentence states the claim, and which provides the supporting findings? Answer: the first sentence is the claim; the second provides facts and details that support it.

problemArchetypes.name: Spot the irrelevant detail
problemArchetypes.example: A speaker is presenting the claim 'Our town needs more bike lanes.' Read the supporting points: (1) 'Three cyclists were injured on Main Street last year.' (2) 'A survey found most residents would bike more if lanes were safer.' (3) 'My cousin has a really fast mountain bike.' Which detail is not pertinent to the claim and should be cut? Answer: point 3, because a personal note about one bike does not support the need for safer lanes.

problemArchetypes.name: Evaluate delivery from a transcript or description
problemArchetypes.example: Read this description of a presentation: 'Tara looked down at her note cards the entire time and read in a very quiet voice. Listeners in the back row said they could not hear her.' Which delivery feature most needs improvement, and what should she do? Answer: volume and eye contact; she should speak louder and look up at the audience while presenting.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the best supporting evidence
problemArchetypes.example: A student claims 'School lunches should include more fresh fruit.' Which choice is the most pertinent and specific supporting detail? (A) 'Fruit is good.' (B) 'A school nurse reported that only one fruit option is offered on most days.' (C) 'I do not like the cafeteria pizza.' (D) 'Lunch is at noon.' Answer: B, because it is a relevant, specific fact that supports the claim.

Easy.description: A short stimulus is embedded in the item: a single claim with two or three short supporting points, a brief outline, or a one to two sentence description of a speaker's delivery (roughly 15 to 40 words total). The task is identify level: pick the claim, choose the obviously irrelevant detail, name which delivery feature is weak, or select the next logical point. Only one concept is tested and the correct answer is clear with no chained reasoning.
constraints: Stimulus is one claim with two or three points, a short list, or a one to two sentence delivery description, all included in the prompt
Tests exactly one concept: sequence, claim versus detail, relevance, or one delivery feature
Identify-level task: select the answer; no explanation required
The off-topic detail or weak delivery feature is obvious; no inference about intended meaning

Medium.description: A longer stimulus is embedded: a four to six point outline to order, a short transcript of several sentences, or a description that combines organization with one or two delivery features (roughly 40 to 80 words). The task is analyze level: arrange points into the most logical sequence, choose the most pertinent of several plausible details, or correct a presentation that mixes a relevance problem with a delivery problem. Distractors are plausible partial answers, such as a sequence that is close but misplaces one point.
constraints: Stimulus is a four to six point outline, a multi-sentence transcript, or a combined organization and delivery scenario in the prompt
Tests sequencing across several points or weighing two or more plausible supporting details
Analyze-level task: order the points or choose and justify the best supporting evidence
Distractors include near-correct sequences or details that are relevant but weaker

Hard.description: A full short scenario is embedded: a transcript or outline of a complete mini presentation of roughly four to seven sentences plus a note on delivery (roughly 80 to 140 words) that contains more than one issue or a subtle one. The task is evaluate level: judge whether the presentation as a whole is logically sequenced and well supported, decide which single revision would most improve it, or explain why a specific detail weakens an otherwise strong case. Requires inference about the speaker's purpose and audience to choose the strongest fix among competing reasonable options.
constraints: Stimulus is a four to seven sentence presentation transcript or outline plus a delivery note, all included in the prompt
Contains multiple or interacting issues: an out-of-order point, an irrelevant detail, and a delivery weakness
Evaluate-level task: select the single best revision and justify it against logic, relevance, or delivery
Requires inference about purpose and audience to pick the strongest improvement among reasonable choices

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats any sentence that sounds confident or general as the claim, confusing a supporting fact for the main point
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels a specific statistic such as 'Test scores rose by ten points' as the claim instead of recognizing the broader position it supports

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student counts a detail as relevant just because it shares a topic word with the claim, ignoring whether it actually supports the claim
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Keeps 'My cousin has a fast bike' as support for 'Our town needs bike lanes' because both mention bikes

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student accepts a personal opinion or feeling as if it were a pertinent fact or detail
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses 'I do not like the cafeteria pizza' or 'Fruit is good' as strong supporting evidence instead of a specific, sourced fact

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student orders points by what is most interesting or dramatic rather than by logical flow from claim to evidence to plan
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Puts the proposed solution or the most exciting fact first, before the claim and the problem it addresses, breaking the logical sequence

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student judges a presentation only by its content and ignores delivery, or judges only delivery and ignores weak content
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Rates a presentation as effective because the facts are correct even though the speaker was inaudible and never looked up, or the reverse

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the delivery features, naming volume when the problem is eye contact or treating speaking fast as the same as speaking unclearly
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Says a speaker who mumbled needs to be louder, or says a speaker who stared at note cards needs clearer pronunciation, instead of naming the correct feature

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes more details always make a stronger presentation, so removing an off-topic point seems wrong
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Argues every listed detail should stay because more evidence is better, instead of cutting the irrelevant one to keep the findings focused
